citations.title: On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics
On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses
On the Uniform Convergence of Relative Frequencies of Events to Their Probabilities

claims.statement: Fisher organized estimation around likelihood, sufficiency, consistency, efficiency, and information, but these concepts do not by themselves choose a data-generating model or guarantee useful prediction.
claims.scope: the definitions and asymptotic program in Fisher's 1922 paper

claims.statement: Neyman and Pearson framed hypothesis testing as a decision rule whose error tradeoffs can be compared between specified alternatives, rather than as a universal measure of evidential truth.
claims.scope: the simple-hypothesis testing problem and its stated extensions

claims.statement: Vapnik and Chervonenkis related uniform empirical convergence to a combinatorial capacity property of a class of events, supplying one route from finite samples to bounded generalization claims.
claims.scope: the formal class-of-events setting of the paper, not every modern learning system

claims.statement: Breiman contrasted data models aimed at interpretable stochastic structure with algorithmic models aimed at predictive performance and argued that empirical evaluation should have a larger role in statistics.
Statistical learning joins distinct questions—estimation, testing, prediction, and generalization—that share probability language but require different objects, loss functions, and warrants.
claims.scope: a curriculum synthesis across the four cited programs

uncertainty: The cited papers represent influential programs, not a complete history of probability, statistics, or learning theory.
Later textbook terminology can make disagreements among estimation, testing, and prediction programs look more unified than they were.
Classical finite-capacity theory does not automatically explain the observed behavior of heavily overparameterized contemporary networks.
limitations: The packet omits Bayesian decision theory, causal inference, information theory, online learning, and many non-Western and applied statistical traditions.
It distinguishes inferential objects conceptually but does not derive every theorem or reproduce empirical examples in full.
A bound stated under explicit assumptions is not evidence that a deployed model satisfies those assumptions or performs safely under distribution shift.
